newsitem.title: UK: UK ad campaign challenges perceptions of disabled.
newsitem.headline: UK ad campaign challenges perceptions of disabled.

text.p: The Co-operative Bank Plc said on Thursday it would launch an advertising campaign challenging both the public and top media executives to think about the way disabled people are perceived and portrayed.

The two adverts, to debut in British cinemas on Friday, were produced by ad agency BDDH for 50,000 pounds ($81,600). The ads were jointly funded by the bank and its Customers Who Care scheme, in which 2.5 pence for every 100 pounds charged to the bank's credit cards is donated to certain charities.

The adverts feature a young man disabled due to thalidomide poisoning and a woman with a facial disfigurement recounting normal incidents in their lives. The strapline is, "See the person not the disability."

David Grayson, chairman of the National Disability Council, told a news conference that there are 6.5 million disabled people in Britain who are trying to get on with leading normal lives and do not want to be thought of as victims or sufferers.

The Co-operative Bank and the National Disability Council said they will also be writing to advertising agencies and film production companies asking them to consider the way disabled people are portrayed. Seminars to examine the extent of the problem will be organised in October, the Co-operative Bank said.
